The Capitol

Dedicated in 166–167 CE to Jupiter, Juno and Minerva for the health of the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus. Its porch of Corinthian columns and pediment still stand to almost full height, the emblem of Dougga.
Square of the Winds

A paved square beside the forum, named after the compass rose carved into its slabs: a circle with the names of twelve winds, such as Septentrio, Africus and Aquilo. Merchants and citizens met here between the temples.

Built in 168–169 CE by a rich citizen, Publius Marcius Quadratus, for about 3,500 spectators. The seats are cut into the hillside and the stage looks over the valley; every summer it hosts a festival of classical theatre.
Temple of Juno Caelestis

Built under Severus Alexander (222–235 CE) for Caelestis, the Roman form of the Punic goddess Tanit. The temple stands in a half-moon court lined with columns, a shape that recalls the crescent of the goddess.
The Libyco-Punic mausoleum

A tower tomb of the 2nd century BCE, about 21 m tall, from the time of the Numidian kings. Its bilingual inscription in Libyc and Punic was cut out in 1842 and is now in the British Museum; the monument was rebuilt from its fallen stones in 1908–1910.
Arch of Severus Alexander
A single-bay arch at the western edge of town, raised in the 3rd century in honour of the emperor Severus Alexander. Another arch, for Septimius Severus, marks the road to Carthage on the east side.
The Licinian Baths
Winter baths of the 3rd century, paid for by the Licinii family. Their walls stand high, and a long vaulted service corridor still runs beneath the halls where slaves stoked the furnaces.
Temple of Saturn
Built in 195 CE at the north-east edge of the town, over an older sanctuary of the Punic god Baal Hammon. A few columns of its porch stand against the sky above the valley.

House of the Hunt

Its underground floor is a courtyard lit by a light well, with Corinthian columns carrying stone architraves. Wealthy families of Bulla Regia dug such floors to escape the summer heat of the plain. The house is named after a hunting mosaic on its upper floor.
House of Amphitrite

Its underground room holds the most famous mosaic of the site: Venus carried over the sea by two sea-centaurs, long taken for the sea-goddess Amphitrite, hence the name. The floor here is a generated pattern; the photo shows the real mosaic, still in place.
House of the Fishing
Thought to be the earliest of the underground houses. Beside a fountain in its basement, a small room has a mosaic of fishermen at work among fish and sea creatures.
The theatre

Built under Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus (161–169 CE), on flat ground with its seats carried on vaults. A 4th-century mosaic of a bear lies in the orchestra. Around 399 Saint Augustine preached here, scolding the townspeople for their love of the shows.
The forum

The paved square at the heart of the town, with the Temple of Apollo on one side and the Capitol on another. Bulla Regia was a royal city of the Numidian kings, hence its name, before it became Roman.
Baths of Julia Memmia
The largest baths of the town, near the entrance, where high walls and arches of the halls still stand.
The Byzantine fort
In the 6th century, when the town had shrunk, the Byzantines built a small fort here from the stones of older buildings.

The minaret

Built in the early 9th century, about 31.5 m tall in three tiers, it is one of the oldest standing minarets in the world. Its square, battered shape became the model for minarets across North Africa and Andalusia.
The courtyard

A vast marble-paved court ringed by arcades of horseshoe arches. It slopes gently towards the centre, where rainwater drains into a great cistern below; the carved well-heads drew it up. A sundial gave the hours of prayer.
The prayer hall

Seventeen naves on hundreds of marble and granite columns, many reused from Roman and Byzantine buildings such as those of Carthage. At the end of the wider central nave, the mihrab is lined with 9th-century lustre tiles from Baghdad, beside the oldest minbar in the Islamic world still in place.
The Aghlabid basins

Built around 862 to store water brought by aqueduct for a city on a dry plain. The large basin, about 128 m across with rounded buttresses all round, held a pavilion on its central pier where the emir could rest.
Mausoleum of Sidi Sahab

The shrine of Abu Zama al-Balawi, a companion of the Prophet, known as "the Barber" because he is said to have kept three hairs of the Prophet’s beard. The 17th-century courts are lined with tiles and carved stucco.
Mosque of the Three Doors

Founded in 866 by Muhammad ibn Khayrun, from Andalusia. Its carved façade, with three arched doors and bands of Kufic inscriptions and floral friezes, is one of the oldest decorated mosque façades in Islamic art.
Bir Barouta

A well dug, by tradition, in the 17th century, in a domed building. Upstairs a blindfolded camel still walks in circles to turn the wheel that raises the water. Legend says it is linked to the well of Zamzam in Mecca.
The ramparts and Bab ech Chouhada
About 3 km of brick ramparts with bastions enclose the medina; most date from the 18th century, on older lines. Bab ech Chouhada, the Gate of the Martyrs, is the main way in from the south.

The Ribat

A fortified monastery of the late 8th century, finished in 821: warrior-monks lived in its cells, prayed and watched the sea for Byzantine ships. It is one of the oldest and best preserved ribats of the North African coast.
Inside the Ribat

Two storeys of cells round a courtyard, with the prayer hall upstairs on the south side. The round watchtower, the nador, rises about 27 m; from its top, fire and smoke signals could be passed along a chain of ribats down the coast.
The Great Mosque

Built in 850–851 under the Aghlabid emir Abu al-Abbas Muhammad, next to the Ribat. With its crenellated walls and corner towers it looks like a fortress; it has no minaret, and the call to prayer was given from the small domed kiosk on a tower. A band of Kufic inscription runs above the courtyard arches.
The Kasbah and the Khalef al-Fata tower
On the highest corner of the medina, the Kasbah guards the town. Its square tower, built in 859 and about 30 m tall, has served as a lighthouse for ships coming into Sousse.
The Archaeological Museum

Inside the Kasbah, around garden courts, one of the finest collections of Roman mosaics after the Bardo in Tunis: sea gods, Bacchus and hunting scenes from Hadrumetum, as Sousse was called in Roman times.
The Kalaout el-Koubba

A medieval hall known for its dome with zigzag ribs, a design found nowhere else in Tunisia. Probably built in the 11th century, it may have been a meeting place or a tomb; today it houses a museum of traditional arts and costumes.
The souks
Covered and open lanes of shops cross the medina from Bab el Gharbi towards the Great Mosque: spices, leather, copper, carpets and jewellery, as in the souks of every Tunisian medina.
The ramparts
About 2.25 km of 9th-century walls still surround the medina, among the best preserved in the Islamic world. Bab el Gharbi, the western gate, leads into the souks.
